entries.clue: Steel, for example, and half of that gold-plated? (6)

indicators.note: plating lays a coat of metal right over a thing, so the covering shows at both ends of what it covers

blocks.note: AU is the chemical symbol for gold
the front half of THat
or is gold in heraldry, the second coat

annotation.walkthrough: One word for gold does the job twice under two different conventions, which is what a plating means: a coat on this side and a coat on that.
annotation.definitionFit: Danielle Steel has written a hundred novels, so the clue defines by example - name one novelist and the general word is wanted.

entries.clue: Skill in pursuit of express plane (8)

indicators.note: to be in pursuit of something is to come along behind it, so the skill trails the piece it chases

blocks.note: to air a grievance is to express it
craft is skill of hand, as in craftsmanship

annotation.walkthrough: 'Express' hides a verb, and the moment you read it as one the surface's fast train falls apart.
annotation.definitionFit: 'Plane' is the everyday shortening of aeroplane, and any aeroplane is an aircraft - one word swapped for its plainer cousin.

entries.clue: Half-heartedly confirm offering support for Tesla's valued helper (8)

indicators.note: done by halves at the heart, so only one of the two letters sitting at the word's centre survives
whatever holds a thing up is underneath it, and in a down clue underneath means later down the entry

blocks.note: T is the symbol for the tesla, the unit of magnetic flux
to reassure is to confirm what someone hoped, and REASSURE with half of its twin middle letters gone leaves this

annotation.walkthrough: The surface points at Nikola Tesla and his indispensable assistant; the wordplay wants only the unit named after him, one letter of it.
annotation.definitionFit: Call a person a treasure and you mean they are precious to have about the place - the word for buried gold used as praise.

entries.clue: Expert putting head down and getting stuck into dealing with Neptune's orbit (5)

indicators.note: the head is the opening letter, and in a down entry sending it down moves it to the foot of its own chunk
a thing stuck into something ends up in the middle of it, with the rest closing over

blocks.note: an ace is an expert at whatever it is
'on' means about - a lecture on birds is one dealing with birds

annotation.walkthrough: 'Head down' is doing two jobs: a diligent worker on the surface, and on the grid a letter with a journey to make.
annotation.definitionFit: Neptune here is the Roman sea god, not the planet, and 'orbit' means sphere of influence - the water is what he rules.

entries.clue: People who dole out corporal punishment and kisses (8)

annotation.definition: People who dole out corporal punishment

blocks.clueFragment: People who dole out corporal punishment
blocks.note: read the verb as striking: anyone who smacks a child is one of these
read the same verb as the noisy sort of kiss, the one you can hear across a room

annotation.walkthrough: Two senses of one verb, with no letters to assemble: to smack is both to strike and to kiss loudly.
annotation.definitionFit: A smacker is a loud kiss, and anyone who smacks is a smacker too - the same agent noun taken from two senses of the verb.

entries.clue: When youth has gone, warehouse's initially replacing learner who helps with deliveries (7)

indicators.note: what a word is initially is the letter it opens with, before anything else arrives
one thing taking another's place leaves the length untouched - a swap, not an extra

blocks.note: the stretch of years after youth is midlife
L is the plate on a learner's car, and it is the letter that goes
the first letter of warehouse moves in to take its place

annotation.walkthrough: L for learner comes off the plates on a British car, and it is worth knowing for good - clues want that letter constantly.
annotation.definitionFit: A midwife delivers babies, so 'deliveries' is the parcel-round joke read the obstetric way.

entries.clue: Crashing car halted building of church (9)

indicators.note: a crash leaves the parts of a car in a heap, and a heap has no order left to it

blocks.note: the nine letters of CAR HALTED put back another way

annotation.walkthrough: Nothing in the surface admits to a place of worship: 'building' reads as work in progress right up until you see it is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A cathedral is the mother church of a diocese, the building holding the bishop's throne - so a church's building names it.

entries.clue: In fairness, gave up drug first before completion of therapy (6)

indicators.note: coming first puts that letter at the head of everything the rest of the clue builds
the completion of a word is the letter it finishes on

blocks.note: E is ecstasy, the crossword's standard drug
to quit is to give up
the closing letter of therapY

annotation.walkthrough: 'First' looks like part of the drug reference and is really positional, telling you where its letter belongs rather than which letter to take.
annotation.definitionFit: Equity is fairness in the legal sense - the branch of law that bends a strict rule when applying it would be unjust.

entries.clue: Carrier picked up by exhausted services for homeless creatures (6)

indicators.note: whatever picks a thing up has hold of it, so what does the lifting closes round what is lifted
an exhausted thing has nothing left in the middle, and only the letters at either end are still standing

blocks.note: the two end letters of ServiceS, the middle used up
a tray is what carries the drinks

annotation.walkthrough: Nothing here is military: 'services' is only a word to hollow out, and 'carrier' wants the thing a waiter holds.
annotation.definitionFit: A stray is an animal that has wandered off and belongs to nobody, so the plural names the cats and dogs living rough.

entries.clue: Fliers postmaster general's carrying around (6)

indicators.note: a phrase that is carrying something holds it inside, letter for letter, straight across the gap between two words
turned around means the run is read from its far end back to its start

blocks.note: postmaSTER GEneral holds the letters, read back up the entry

annotation.walkthrough: A reversed hidden word is the hardest of all to spot, because the letters are sitting in plain sight and only the direction of travel is odd.
annotation.definitionFit: Egrets are the small white herons of marsh and estuary, and 'fliers' defines them the loose way - by what any bird does.

entries.clue: Notoriously thirsty thespian drinking gallons in lake showed up again (2-7)

indicators.note: someone drinking takes what is in front of him right inside himself, so this piece closes over the rest
'in' does the simplest containment job in the language - the gallons go inside the lake

blocks.note: Oliver Reed, the actor as famous for drinking as for acting
G is the abbreviation for gallons
a mere is a lake - Windermere is one

annotation.walkthrough: The enumeration (2-7) is a tip in itself: a hyphen after two letters nearly always means a prefix, and here it is the one meaning again.
annotation.definitionFit: To re-emerge is to come back into view after a spell out of sight, which is what showing up a second time describes.

entries.clue: Straighter French street runs through outskirts of Tréguier (5)

indicators.note: a road running through a town goes in one side and out the other, with the town wrapped round it
the outskirts are the edges of a place - its first and last letters, with everything between left behind

blocks.note: the first and last letters of Tréguier
rue is the French for street

annotation.walkthrough: Tréguier is a real Breton town, which is why a French street sits so comfortably inside it.
annotation.definitionFit: A truer edge is a straighter one - 'true' in the carpenter's sense of properly aligned, not the sense of factually correct.

entries.clue: Hardened sap to offend another time? (5)

blocks.note: RE- is the prefix that means over again
to sin is to offend against a commandment

annotation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the joke: to offend a second time would be to re-sin, a word no dictionary carries but the letters do.
annotation.definitionFit: Resin is the sticky stuff that seeps from a pine and sets solid, so the definition names it by its source and its state at once.

entries.clue: Bump into nasty Yankee apparently (9)

indicators.note: 'into' drives one thing right inside another rather than leaving it alongside

blocks.note: evil is nasty at full strength
Y is Yankee in the NATO alphabet
a bump in a car door is a dent

annotation.walkthrough: Yankee for Y comes from the NATO alphabet, which will supply a letter for any clue that needs one - Alpha, Bravo, Charlie and the rest.
annotation.definitionFit: Evidently and apparently are both adverbs meaning 'on the evidence in front of you', so one drops straight into the other's place.

entries.clue: Out of uniform, alien visitors taking breather inside woods (7)

indicators.note: out of uniform means the uniform is off, so the letter standing for it leaves too
a piece taken inside settles among the other letters instead of beside them

blocks.note: unidentified flying objects are the visitors from elsewhere
U is uniform in the NATO alphabet, and this is the letter that leaves
taking a breather is having a rest

annotation.walkthrough: 'Out of uniform' reads as soldiers off duty and does its real work by stripping a single letter from the flying saucers.
annotation.definitionFit: A forest is a great stretch of trees, so 'woods' is the ordinary word for the same country in the plural.

entries.clue: Occasionally call for assistance covering personal break (9)

indicators.note: a cover goes over the top of a thing and round its sides, leaving it wrapped

blocks.note: the distress call is SOS
me-time is time kept for yourself

annotation.walkthrough: Me-time is new enough that it still looks like surface chat, and the distress call splits cleanly round it.
annotation.definitionFit: Sometimes and occasionally are both adverbs for 'now and then', differing only in register.

entries.clue: Be paid to study but not back in school (4)

indicators.note: 'but not' takes away whatever follows it, so that letter never reaches the grid
the back of a word is the letter it ends on, and 'in' says which word to take it from

blocks.note: to study a subject is to learn it
the final letter of schooL, the one to drop

annotation.walkthrough: 'Back in school' looks like one phrase about term starting and is really two instructions: which end of a word, and which word.
annotation.definitionFit: To earn is to be paid for work done - the verb on the payslip, describing the getting rather than the money.

entries.clue: Originally, offers by upwardly mobile online marketplace confined to hospital food (4,4)

indicators.note: what a word is originally is the letter it starts from, before the rest of it happens
letters travelling upwards in a down entry are read from the bottom back to the top
someone confined to a place cannot get out of it, so these letters are shut in on both sides

blocks.note: the opening letter of offers
eBay is the online marketplace, climbing the entry
a san, short for sanatorium, is the sickbay in every boarding school

annotation.walkthrough: SAN for hospital is worth pocketing: it comes from sanatorium and turns up wherever a clue wants three letters for a ward.
annotation.definitionFit: The soya bean is the pulse behind tofu and soy sauce, so 'food' defines it by the general class it belongs to.

entries.clue: Base spread evenly over broken slate (8)

indicators.note: taking a word evenly means the letters standing in the even places, second, fourth and sixth
in a down entry whatever is over something is written above it, so it comes first
something broken is in pieces, and pieces can be fitted together in another order

blocks.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters of sPrEaD
the five letters of slate rebuilt

annotation.walkthrough: 'Spread evenly' is one phrase with two jobs: a breakfast-table picture on the surface, and an instruction to count letters in twos.
annotation.definitionFit: A pedestal is the base a statue or a column stands on, so the definition is the architectural word in plain English.

entries.clue: Cheeky devils - one's hugging representative (4)

indicators.note: a hug closes all the way round whatever is being held, so one piece finishes up inside the other

blocks.note: one is the single stroke I, and the 's comes along with it
your representative in the Commons is an MP

annotation.walkthrough: An apostrophe-s left standing at the end is a favourite way of handing over two letters, and it stays put while the other piece moves in.
annotation.definitionFit: An imp is a small mischievous demon, and 'cheeky' picks the fairy-tale sort rather than the fire-and-brimstone sort.

entries.clue: Back amendment of Spooner’s, losing vote in the end (7)

indicators.note: an amendment alters the wording of a thing, and what is altered here is the order the letters stand in
what is lost is dropped before anything else is done with the rest
the end of a word is its final letter, and that is the one being given up

blocks.note: the reverend's name with its 's, eight letters to start from
the last letter of votE, the one that goes

annotation.walkthrough: Spooner is the red herring of the puzzle: no sounds are swapped anywhere, and his name is simply the fodder, one letter lighter.
annotation.definitionFit: To sponsor a bill or a runner is to back it - 'back' in the money-behind-you sense rather than the direction.

entries.clue: We'll shortly attend reception (7)

indicators.note: 'shortly' cuts a word short, taking the last letter off the one it follows

blocks.note: WE'LL run together is WELL, docked of its final letter
to attend a party is to come to it

annotation.walkthrough: The apostrophe is the whole disguise: 'We'll' is a promise on the surface and four letters to trim in the wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: A welcome is the reception an arrival is given - 'a warm welcome' and 'a warm reception' are the same greeting.

entries.clue: Aussie native's bill cut up (6)

indicators.note: in a down clue 'up' sends the letters back the way they came, read from the foot of the entry towards the top

blocks.note: the bill run up at a bar is the tab
to cut the grass is to mow it

annotation.walkthrough: A whole charade can be turned at once rather than piece by piece: build the two words in clue order, then read the lot upwards.
annotation.definitionFit: The wombat is a burrowing marsupial found nowhere but Australia, so 'Aussie native' names it as one of the continent's own.

entries.clue: I reach out and it's more painful (6)

indicators.note: 'out' here means out of true rather than absent - the letters are not standing in the arrangement they were handed over in

blocks.note: the six letters of I REACH in a fresh order

annotation.walkthrough: The surface sounds like a confession about stretching too far, and every word of it except the definition is either fodder or the nudge to shuffle it.
annotation.definitionFit: Achier is the comparative of achy - one thing hurting more dully than another, the way muscles do the day after.

entries.clue: Excursion got uni in trouble (6)

indicators.note: a thing in trouble is in a mess, and a mess is letters lying in no proper order

blocks.note: the six letters of GOT UNI rearranged

annotation.walkthrough: 'Uni' is modern enough to pass as student chatter, which is exactly why it goes unnoticed as fodder.
annotation.definitionFit: An outing is a short trip taken for pleasure - a day at the seaside - which is what an excursion is.

entries.clue: Royal gathering fell back where bench is (9)

indicators.note: an across entry runs left to right, so coming back means these letters are read the other way along the row

blocks.note: the court is the monarch's household gathered round
a fell is northern moorland

annotation.walkthrough: 'Fell' is a noun here, a Lakeland hill, and not the past tense of fall the surface is selling.
annotation.definitionFit: The Bench means the judges collectively, so the place where the bench sits to hear a case is what the clue points at.

entries.clue: Old Scottish lord occupying Elizabethan estate (5)

indicators.note: whatever occupies a space is sitting inside it, and one word's letters are sitting inside two others here

blocks.note: ElizabeTHAN Estate carries the letters straight across the gap between the words

annotation.walkthrough: Shakespeare put the word in everybody's head, and the setter has hidden it inside a queen from the wrong century entirely.
annotation.definitionFit: A thane held land from a Scottish or Anglo-Saxon king - Macbeth is Thane of Cawdor - so the title belongs to history.

entries.clue: Article has limited space for subject (5)

indicators.note: to limit a thing is to fence it in on either side, which is where the smaller piece has to go

blocks.note: the definite article
an em is the printer's space, as wide as the letter M is

annotation.walkthrough: Printers measure spaces in ems and ens, after the widths of M and N, and that little pair turns up in clues constantly once you know it.
annotation.definitionFit: A theme is what a piece of music or writing is about - the subject running through the whole of it rather than one topic among many.

entries.clue: Man introduced by retiring police officer displaying unique turn of phrase (5)

indicators.note: to retire is to go back the way you came, so these two letters are read in the other direction
whatever introduces something comes in ahead of it, so that piece leads the way

blocks.note: a DI is a detective inspector, turned round here
IOM is how the Isle of Man writes itself on an address

annotation.walkthrough: 'Man' is the island rather than the male, and the clue hides that by standing a person and a policeman on either side of it.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom is a fixed expression whose sense you cannot work out from its words - 'kick the bucket' - so it is phrasing peculiar to one language.

entries.clue: Custer essentially had soldiers close to fort position at bank (9)

indicators.note: the essence of a word is its middle, the letters at its heart rather than the ones on show at the edges
close to a word means the far end of it, the letter it closes with

blocks.note: the middle pair of cuSTer
had lunch is ate lunch
soldiers are men under arms
the closing letter of forT

annotation.walkthrough: Custer's last stand supplies the whole surface, and 'had' is the piece most solvers walk past - a past tense about eating, not possession.
annotation.definitionFit: A bank statement sets out where an account stands, so 'position at bank' names the document by the financial position it reports.

entries.clue: Judge once more screening foreign fighter's record collection (8)

indicators.note: a screen is put in front of something to keep it out of sight, so those letters end up covered by the others

blocks.note: to judge a case a second time is to retry it
a GI is an American soldier, foreign from here, and the 's rides along

annotation.walkthrough: GI comes from 'government issue', stamped on American kit, and it has meant an American soldier ever since.
annotation.definitionFit: A registry is where official records are kept together - births, marriages and deaths gathered in one place.

entries.clue: Core group of mariners trapped by bottom of boat (6)

indicators.note: anything trapped is held on every side, so this piece is shut inside the other one

blocks.note: the keel is the timber running along a boat's bottom
the Royal Navy is RN

annotation.walkthrough: 'Bottom of boat' looks like an instruction to take a final letter and is nothing of the kind - it is a plain synonym.
annotation.definitionFit: The kernel is the edible middle of a nut, and by extension the core of an argument - one word doing both jobs.
